threads_text: China's DeepSeek and Moonshot AI reportedly trained their newest models on answers from OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, The Information reports. It's called distillation, and OpenAI, Anthropic and Google all say it lets rivals copy them on the cheap. Is training on another AI's answers fair game or theft?

paragraphs.text: Chinese AI developers DeepSeek and Moonshot AI relied heavily on outputs from OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model to train their latest models, The Information reported on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, citing people with direct knowledge of the matter. Reuters and Finimize both carried the report.

According to the report, two recent releases benefited from the practice: Moonshot AI's Kimi K3.1 Pro, which came out the week before the report, and DeepSeek's upgraded V4.1-Flash 1017, which launched on October 17.
OpenAI, DeepSeek and Moonshot AI did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters.

The technique at the center of the report is called distillation. A developer sends large numbers of prompts to a stronger model and uses its answers as training data for a different model. Finimize described it as a way to copy capabilities without paying the full cost of the original research.

Reuters described distillation as a flashpoint in the technology competition between the United States and China. Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have all argued that it lets rivals reproduce advanced capabilities more quickly and at lower cost.
Earlier warnings from OpenAI and Anthropic

The report follows an earlier disclosure by OpenAI. In a blog post on September 30, 2026, the company said it had linked a core part of a distillation campaign that began in July to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, according to Reuters.

Anthropic has described similar pressure on its own models. Earlier in October, the company said new measures against distillation attacks on its Claude models had cut the amount of data harvested by about 90 to 99 percent, Reuters and Finimize reported.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the report shows how hard it is for a model maker to protect its work once the model is open to paying customers. Every answer a public model gives can, in principle, become training material for someone else. Defenses such as the ones Anthropic described reduce that flow but do not appear to stop it entirely, and the companies involved have not publicly confirmed the specific claims about Kimi K3.1 Pro and V4.1-Flash 1017.

Finimize expects AI providers to respond with more monitoring, tighter rate limits and restrictions on outputs. That could mean stricter usage checks and more identity verification for legitimate customers who send high volumes of requests, along with higher compliance costs that may eventually reach the price of AI tools.

The next thing to watch is whether OpenAI confirms the report or announces new limits on how GPT-6 Astra can be accessed, and whether DeepSeek or Moonshot AI responds publicly to the claims about their October releases. A public answer from any of the three companies would show how far each is willing to go in a dispute that so far has played out mostly through blog posts and anonymous sourcing.
